expR-plane-predicts: Plane predicts: ≤ 180.0000° — exactly 180 with straight rays, less if light bends down
expR-globe-predicts: Globe predicts: 180° + γ(1−k) — an excess that grows with distance
expR-verd-exceeds: Sum exceeds 180°. No flat arrangement can do this: on a plane the verticals are parallel, so straight rays give exactly 180.000° and downward-bending rays give less. The excess here is {am}, {plaus}
expR-plaus-ok: and k = {k} sits inside the measured range 0.10–0.34, so nothing exotic is being assumed.
expR-plaus-bad: though k = {k} is outside the ordinary measured range 0.10–0.34 — worth re-checking the angles or the clock.
expR-verd-exact: Sum is exactly 180°. This is the flat prediction with straight rays. Repeat it on a longer line: the globe's excess grows in proportion to s, so a 100 km line should show about {am} at k = 0.13. A run of exact 180s across several baselines would falsify this page.
expR-verd-below: Sum is below 180°. That is on the plane's side of the line — and it is also what a globe gives if k > 1, i.e. inside a duct. Before concluding anything, check simultaneity and repeat at another hour: a single sub-180 sum over a warm surface is the classic signature of a mis-timed pair.

Both night curves pass k equal to one, the air in which a globe looks flat, below a few metres

rb-fx-alt: Temperature against height from the sea to 41.6 m, for five airs over the same sea at 14.6 °C, with the wind and humidity of 28 March 2026: the air at 2 m three, two and one kelvin colder than the sea, as warm as the sea, and half a kelvin warmer. The colder the air, the faster the temperature falls in the lowest metres; above about ten metres every curve falls slowly.

rs-fx-alt: A horizontal scale of temperature gradient. A black mark with a grey band is the gradient of the day's air and its uncertainty; a coloured mark with its band is the gradient a model needs for the photograph. The distance between the two marks, divided by the half-widths of the two bands facing each other, combined, is z.
